PRESCHOOL · AGE 3 · CLASS 3 MAGIC GAME

Magic Shape Builder

Five pictures are built from shapes: a house, a rocket, a tree, a robot and a butterfly. Pick a picture, then tap the shapes into place — circle, square, triangle and friends. Grown-ups read the words; little ones do the building.

No scores, no timers — just building.

STEP 2 · CHOOSE A DESIGN

What shall we build today?

Tap a picture to build it. You can build as many as you like — the shapes never run out.

OFF-SCREEN PLAY

Shapes you can hold.

The best shape set costs nothing: cut, sort and stack with what you already have. Pick one of these and let your child lead.

Paper shape cutouts

  • Cut circles, squares, triangles and rectangles from paper or old magazines — then rebuild the house or the rocket on the table, just like on the screen.

Household shape hunt

  • Build a picture from household objects: a plate circle, a book rectangle, a corner triangle. Photograph the result for your own art wall.

Snack shapes

  • Crackers, banana slices and cheese triangles are building materials too. Build, name each shape, then eat the architecture.

One safety word for this game: grown-ups handle scissors for the cutouts, and snack builds use foods your child already eats safely — cut grapes small, and sit down together to build and munch.

ACTIVITY COMPLETE

Shapes in all the right places!

Circles, squares, rectangles, triangles and ovals are now your child’s building blocks — on the screen, on the table and around the house. Whether you built one design or all five, that was real shape practice, and there was never a score to worry about.

FOR GROWN-UPS

How building teaches shapes.

Every board shows dashed outlines where each shape belongs, and the tray holds exactly the shapes the design needs. A shape only clicks into a spot that matches its form — a triangle will not fit a circle spot — so every placement is a small piece of real shape reasoning. After two misses the board gently pulses an empty spot that fits the shape in hand: a hint, never a correction.

The reference picture stays beside the board on purpose: comparing the picture with the work-in-progress is the actual skill — looking carefully, checking, trying again. Naming each shape out loud when it lands (the game does it; so can you) is what turns play into vocabulary.

Tap-to-place works with mouse, touch and keyboard: pieces and spots are real buttons. And the paper-cutout version in Off-Screen Play is where the shapes become something your child can hold.
